name: The Just-World Hypothesis
statement: People need to believe the world is fair, so they decide victims must deserve their fate.
meaning: People have a need to believe the world is fundamentally fair: that people get what they deserve and deserve what they get. Because evidence of undeserved suffering threatens this belief, they often defend it by rationalising the injustice away, most strikingly by blaming or devaluing victims so their misfortune appears deserved. The belief in a just world is thus both a comfort and a source of cruelty toward the unlucky.
mechanism: The belief functions as a kind of contract with the world: if effort is reliably rewarded and wrongdoing punished, one can plan and strive with confidence. Confronted with suffering that has no just cause, people can respond rationally (accept the injustice, help the victim, or make restitution) or non-rationally, by denying, withdrawing, or reinterpreting the suffering as deserved. When helping or compensation is impossible, derogating the victim becomes the main way to keep the belief intact, which is why even sympathetic observers may turn against those they cannot aid.

examples.text: In Lerner's classic experiment, observers watching a woman apparently receive random electric shocks came to devalue her the more she suffered, but not when told she would be compensated, showing derogation restores the sense of a just world.
Strong believers tend to blame the poor for poverty, assault victims for their assault, and the ill for their illness, reinterpreting bad luck as deserved.
Everyday forms include belief in karma and the conviction that hard work always pays off, each casting outcomes as morally earned.

variants.name: Personal versus general belief
variants.text: Belief that the world is just for oneself predicts optimism, coping, and well-being, while belief that it is just for people in general is more tied to victim-blaming and harsh social judgement.

variants.name: The Just World Scale
variants.text: Rubin and Peplau's 1975 measure of how strongly a person holds the belief, which varies across people and correlates with authoritarianism, the work ethic, and religiosity.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most studied phenomena in social psychology, explaining the otherwise puzzling tendency to blame victims and to rationalise inequality. It illuminates reactions to poverty, illness, and assault, and its dual nature (a belief that both motivates striving and licenses cruelty) makes it central to understanding how people preserve their sense of a fair world in the face of a plainly unfair one.

working.text: read victim-blaming not always as simple malice but often as a motivated defence of the need to believe the world is fair.
recognise that when observers can help or compensate a victim, they are less likely to derogate them.
distinguish belief in justice for oneself, which tends to aid well-being, from belief in justice for all, which fuels harsh judgement.

limits: It is a well-established phenomenon but carries the usual social-psychology caveats: effect sizes and moderators vary across studies, samples, and which scale is used, and measurement across the competing scales is contested. There is real cultural variation, the belief being weaker where people experience relative powerlessness, and the research is concentrated in a few Western countries. As with much classic mid-century social psychology, the field-wide replication scrutiny applies, though the landmark study has not been specifically overturned. And the belief is not purely a fallacy: it has adaptive functions, buffering stress and motivating goal pursuit.
misreadings: It is not simply an irrational fallacy: the belief has documented adaptive and motivational functions, and the 'fundamental delusion' phrase is Lerner's rhetorical title, not a claim that it is uniformly harmful. It is not one single thing either: belief in justice for oneself and for others behave very differently. And victim-blaming is not merely cruelty or ignorance; the theory's point is that it is a motivated defence of a needed belief, occurring even in otherwise sympathetic people.
origin: Developed by the social psychologist Melvin Lerner from the 1960s, whose experiments on reactions to an innocent victim, beginning with Lerner and Simmons in 1966, led to his 1980 book 'The Belief in a Just World: A Fundamental Delusion'; the standard measure is Rubin and Peplau's Just World Scale (1975).

sources.text: Lerner & Simmons, "Observer's reaction to the 'innocent victim': compassion or rejection?" Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 4(2):203-210 (1966). — the foundational experiment and the compensation condition.
Hafer & Begue, "Experimental research on just-world theory: Problems, developments, and future challenges," Psychological Bulletin (2005). — the review of the evidence and its caveats.
Just-world hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the statement, Lerner's history, the personal-versus-general distinction, and cultural variation.
